fast.topic: Week 3, taught by Abimbola Oyarinu, runs in three strands from first European contact to formal British occupation. The first is the Portuguese incursion into the Niger Area: sailors seeking new markets began exploring the West African coast in the early 15th century, improving seafaring techniques and ship design with the caravel, and Portugal then dominated world trade for nearly 200 years on fabrics, spices and gold; the incursion opened the area to the rest of the world and eventually led to colonialism and exploitation, caused a series of wars to keep up the supply of slaves, contributed to the abandonment of African cultures, played a major role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, and along the Nigerian coast fed the growth of brass casting in Benin and the emergence of trading in the Lagos Lagoon. The second strand is the slave trade itself, with the triangular route the Portuguese developed (Africa the source, the Americas the destination, Europeans the organisers), Phillip Curtin on the largest intercontinental migration in western history spanning 300 years, the Pope's division of the Old World, the Spanish Asiento, the 1527 Puerto Rico uprising, the Dutch joining in the 17th century and the British becoming biggest in the 18th, a Middle Passage of 5 to 8 weeks with each slave allotted 6ft by 1ft by 4 inches on ships of 451 to 600, smallpox, dysentery and ophthalmia, over 15 million reaching the Americas, Paul Lovejoy's over 7 million dying in transit, and the verdicts of Wole Soyinka, Walter Rodney, Washington Alcott and Claude Ake. Abolition follows: British seizure of slave ships from 1792 with repatriation to Sierra Leone, and Thomas Fowell Buxton's 1833 bill arguing the trade had to be stopped from Africa itself. The third strand opens with the Bight of Benin as the last slaving centre by 1840 and Lagos as the leading slave port, Beecroft's 1849 appointment as the start of direct British influence, the 1851 treaty with Kosoko, his refusal, the bombardment, Akitoye's restoration on 29 December 1851 with Kosoko fleeing to Epe, the 1852 trade treaty, and the annexation of Lagos in 1861. It then follows company rule: Macgregor Laird's 1857 expedition and the ports of Ado, Onitsha and Gbebe, his Central African Company of 1858 and death in 1861, the River Niger Navigation and Trading Company of 1862, and the amalgamation into the United African Company under Sir George Goldie-Taubman, renamed the National African Company after buying two rival French firms. It closes with Consul Hewett's 1884 treaty-making tour and the Berlin Conference, the charter sequence of 1881, 1882 and 1886 that created the Royal Niger Company, its control of the Niger basin by 1887, critics Harry Johnston, Ajayi Crowther and Hoenigsberg against the protection of Colonial Secretary Salisbury, the Oil River Protectorate of 1884 with its seven districts renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate in 1893, and the decline through Sir Ralph Moor's 1891 appointment, price wars, smuggling, Joseph Chamberlain's appointment, the Brass raid on Akassa, the Kirk Commission and the revocation of the charter.

fast.topic: This week covers HTML, the HyperText Markup Language used to structure web pages with tags. It starts with the document skeleton: the declaration as the first line, the root element, the invisible holding , , <link> and <script>, and the <body> holding visible content. It then works through the content elements: headings <h1> to <h6>, <p>, links <a> with the href attribute, ordered <ol> and unordered <ul> lists, <img> with src and alt, <div> as a block container and <span> as an inline one, tables built from <table>, <tr>, <th> and <td>, definition lists from <dl>, <dt> and <dd>, plus <button>, audio and video, semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, section, footer), <iframe>, <br>, comments, and the text-formatting elements <strong>, <em> and <u>. Hyperlinks are treated in depth: anchor text, URLs, text, image and button links, navigation menus, internal links using relative URLs, same-page anchors using href="#id" with the id attribute, external links with the full http:// or https:// URL, and target="_blank" to open in a new tab. Web forms follow: the <form> element with its action attribute (where the data is sent) and method attribute (GET, which appends data to the URL as query parameters, versus POST, which sends it in the request body). The common controls are input type text, password, email, radio and checkbox, plus <select>, <textarea> and <button>, governed by the attributes name, id, value, placeholder, required, disabled, maxlength, min, max and multiple. It closes with HTML5 validation attributes (required, min and max, minlength and maxlength, and pattern for regular expressions), file uploads using <input type="file"> with enctype="multipart/form-data", and accessibility using <label>, alternative text, and <fieldset> with <legend>.

deep.topic: Computational approaches to problem solving, treated conceptually. This session covers what a computational approach is and the three factors (clear definition, computability, data requirements) that decide whether one can be used; the mechanism and cost of each of the eleven named approaches — problem recognition, backtracking, data mining, performance testing, pipelining, visualisation, brute force, divide and conquer, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming and hypothesis testing. The emphasis is on why each approach works, what it costs, and the conditions under which it fails: the divide-and-conquer recombination condition, the greedy algorithm's lack of an optimality guarantee against dynamic programming's guarantee, and the meaning of significance level and p-value in the accept/reject rule. It does not ask for traces or worked arithmetic; that is Saturday.

fast.topic: This week covers how sentences are analysed and how words are classed. A sentence is defined as a group of words expressing a complete thought, requiring a subject (noun or pronoun) and a predicate (verb), and it is analysed in two ways: by function (its purpose) and by structure (how it is built from subjects, predicates, objects, nouns and verbs). The four structural types are simple (one independent clause), compound (two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, so, or by a semicolon), complex (one independent clause plus at least one dependent or subordinate clause, usually introduced by although, because, while or since), and compound-complex (two or more independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause). The lesson gives five tips for building compound-complex sentences: relative clauses, parenthesis, context clues, punctuation (semicolon, hyphen), and details and explanations, all in service of writing a healthy paragraph. The four functional types are declarative (statements), imperative (commands, instructions, requests), interrogative (questions) and exclamatory (strong emotion), with conditional 'if' sentences given as an additional fifth category expressing a condition and its likely result. The second half divides words into function words and content words: function words (also called grammatical, structure, empty or form words) carry little meaning alone and comprise conjunctions, auxiliary or helping verbs, prepositions, articles and pronouns, plus modals, qualifiers and question words. Content words, or lexical words, carry the main meaning and comprise nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs. The key discriminator to remember is stress: content words are emphasised in speech while function words remain non-stressed, and Pennebaker's figure is that function words are under one-tenth of one percent of vocabulary but almost 60 percent of words actually used. The third strand of the week is concord, the set of rules governing agreement between different elements in a sentence: subject-verb agreement is the fundamental rule, requiring the number of the subject to match the number of the verb, while the Rule of Proximity Agreement is the harder case, requiring the verb or noun to align with the closest subject when a sentence has several subject elements. The presence of 'or' (or 'nor') in the subject decides whether the verb is singular or plural, in contrast with 'and', which normally makes the subject plural, so students must read sentence structure carefully before choosing the verb.

deep.topic: The same Week 3 limit material worked as problems: reading a limit, substituting first, and classifying what comes back as a number, as a non-zero over zero, or as an indeterminate 0/0 or infinity/infinity. Choosing among direct substitution, factorization and cancellation, conjugate rationalization for radicals, clearing a compound fraction, dividing by the highest power for limits at infinity, and L'Hopital's Rule, then executing the chosen route accurately. Checking a finished answer for plausibility, including sign analysis of one-sided infinite limits. Diagnosing two standard wrong routes: applying L'Hopital to a quotient that was never indeterminate, and using the quotient rule in place of L'Hopital.

fast.topic: This week's practical studies the non-linear relationship between current and voltage in a non-ohmic resistor, using a voltmeter, an ammeter, a DC power supply and a resistor made of either tungsten or iron selected from a drop-down list. After inspecting the circuit and choosing the material, the applied voltage is set from 0.1 V upwards and the Record button saves the voltmeter reading V and the current I at each step, covering the whole range up to 50 V, after which an Excel sheet of the data downloads automatically. Plotting I against V gives a curve rather than a straight line, showing that V/I is not constant and the resistor does not obey Ohm's law. The recorded values are then used to compute I squared and the power P = IV, and plotting P against I squared gives a straight line whose gradient is the resistance, verifying Joule's law P = I squared R. The conclusion is that current flowing through the conductor generates heat, the resulting temperature rise changes the resistance, and this is why the current-voltage response of a tungsten filament becomes non-linear at higher currents.

checks.topic: Limits treated conceptually: what the object lim(x to a) f(x) = L actually asserts, and why it is a statement about the values of f on a punctured neighbourhood of a rather than about f(a). Covers the epsilon-delta formulation and the order in which delta responds to epsilon, one-sided limits and the two-sided existence criterion, and the three-part definition of continuity. Covers why each limit law carries the hypothesis it does: the quotient and reciprocal laws needing a non-zero denominator limit, the composite law needing continuity of the outer function, and the Squeeze Theorem needing both bounds to share a limit. Also covers what the word indeterminate means for 0/0, and why cancelling a factor that vanishes at a is legitimate inside a limit.

questions.q: The statement lim(x to a) f(x) = L is a claim about which values of f?
options: The single value f(a), which the statement asserts is equal to L.
The value f(a) together with the values at points near a, which are averaged to give L.
The values of f at points near a, with the point x = a itself excluded from consideration.
The values of f across its entire domain, of which L is the overall trend.
questions.concept: The limit is defined on a punctured neighbourhood: f(a) is irrelevant to it.
questions.why: The definition quantifies over x with 0 < |x - a| < delta, which deliberately omits x = a, so f(a) may be undefined or equal to anything without affecting L.

questions.q: In the epsilon-delta definition of a limit, how are epsilon and delta related?
options: A challenger supplies epsilon first, and delta must then be produced small enough that every x within delta of a, other than a, has f(x) within epsilon of L.
A challenger supplies delta first, and epsilon must then be made wide enough that the band around L contains all the values f takes near a.
Epsilon and delta are picked independently of one another, and the definition is satisfied as soon as one pair of them happens to work.
Epsilon is determined by the shape of the function and delta is determined by the point a, so neither is genuinely chosen.
questions.concept: The logical order of the quantifiers: for every epsilon there exists delta.
questions.why: The definition reads 'for all epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0', so delta is a response to an arbitrary epsilon; reversing the order or decoupling the two destroys the meaning.

questions.q: In lim(x to 2) (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2), why may the factor (x - 2) be cancelled even though it is zero at x = 2?
options: Because 0/0 is equal to 1, so the repeated factor contributes a factor of one to the value.
Because the limit laws allow cancellation whenever the numerator and denominator share a common root.
Because the function is implicitly redefined at x = 2, which makes the cancellation valid at that point.
Because the limit only consults values with x not equal to 2, and at every such x the ratio (x - 2)/(x - 2) is genuinely 1.
questions.concept: Cancellation is licensed by the punctured neighbourhood, not by any algebraic identity at the point itself.
questions.why: The simplified function x + 2 agrees with the original at every x except x = 2, and since the limit never inspects x = 2, the two have the same limit there.

questions.q: To call the form 0/0 'indeterminate' is to say that
options: the limit must be zero, since the numerator is heading to zero.
the form by itself fixes nothing: different pairs of functions producing this form have different limits, so the functions must be examined.
the limit definitely fails to exist, since division by zero is undefined.
the limit exists but can never be found by algebraic means, only numerically.
questions.concept: Indeterminate means underdetermined by the form, not non-existent and not automatically zero.
questions.why: x^2/x, x/x and x/x^3 all give 0/0 at 0 yet have limits 0, 1 and infinity respectively, so the symbol 0/0 carries no information about the answer.

questions.q: Suppose lim(x to a) f(x) = L exists. What further condition does continuity of f at a demand?
options: That f be differentiable at a, since continuity is the weaker half of differentiability.
That the left-hand and right-hand limits at a agree, which the mere existence of L does not guarantee.
That f(a) be defined and be equal to L.
That f(a) be defined, with the particular value it takes being immaterial.
questions.concept: The three-part definition of continuity, and which part the existence of the limit already supplies.
questions.why: Existence of L already forces the one-sided limits to agree; continuity adds that f(a) exists and matches L, which is exactly what rules out a hole or a misplaced point.

questions.q: The quotient law lim(f/g) = (lim f)/(lim g) is stated with the hypothesis lim g not equal to 0. What actually breaks without it?
options: The right-hand side L/M is not a number when M = 0, and the genuine limit may then be any real number, plus or minus infinity, or non-existent, depending on f.
The product law would be contradicted, because a product of two limits can never come out as zero.
The function g would cease to be continuous at a, so no limit law at all could be quoted for it.
The limit of f would be forced to be zero as well, so the quotient would always be the form 0/0.
questions.concept: Why the hypotheses of a limit law are not decoration: the conclusion is literally ill-formed without them.
questions.why: With M = 0 the expression L/M names nothing, and examples such as x^2/x, x/x and 1/x at 0 show every possible behaviour arising, so no single conclusion can be drawn.

questions.q: The Squeeze Theorem requires the two bounding functions to have the same limit at a. Why is that requirement essential?
options: Because the proof adds the two bounds together, an operation that is only valid when they are equal.
Because f has to sit exactly midway between the bounds, which is false when their limits differ.
Because if the bounds have different limits then f is no longer trapped between them and the inequalities cease to hold.
Because f is only known to lie somewhere in the gap between the bounds, and only when that gap shrinks to a single number is f forced to any particular value.
questions.concept: The Squeeze Theorem works by trapping, so its power comes entirely from the trap closing.
questions.why: The inequalities confine f to the interval between the bounds; if that interval tends to a non-degenerate range, f could approach any point of it or oscillate, so no limit follows.

questions.q: The composite rule lim(x to a) g(f(x)) = g(L), where L = lim(x to a) f(x), assumes g is continuous at L. What goes wrong if g has a jump at L?
options: f(x) might never reach L exactly, so the inner limit is never actually attained.
f(x) approaches L without necessarily equalling it, and a jump at L means the values of g just beside L need not approach g(L).
The composite g(f(x)) becomes undefined for all x sufficiently close to a.
The derivative g'(L) fails to exist, so no limit law can be applied to the composite.
questions.concept: Why continuity of the outer function is what licenses moving a limit inside it.
questions.why: The inner values f(x) sit near L but generally not at L, so the composite is governed by g's behaviour near L; only continuity guarantees those nearby values of g approach g(L).

questions.q: Explain why the value f(a) can be altered to any number whatsoever without changing lim(x to a) f(x).
questions.concept: The limit is a property of a punctured neighbourhood.
questions.why: A full answer says that the definition only constrains x satisfying 0 < |x - a| < delta, which excludes x = a; so the truth of |f(x) - L| < epsilon for those x is untouched by redefining f at a. It should add the consequence: a limit can exist where f(a) is undefined (a removable discontinuity), and f(a) can be defined yet differ from the limit, which is precisely why continuity has to be stated as a separate condition rather than following from the limit.

questions.q: Explain why 0/0 is called indeterminate but 5/0 is not, in terms of what each form tells you about the competing behaviours.
questions.concept: Indeterminacy as a contest between two effects, versus a form whose outcome is already settled.
questions.why: A full answer explains that in 0/0 two forces oppose each other: a numerator shrinking to zero pushes the quotient down while a denominator shrinking to zero pushes it up, and the winner depends on the relative rates, so the form alone settles nothing. Concrete rate examples such as x^2/x, x/x and x/x^3 at 0 giving 0, 1 and infinity should be offered. For 5/0 there is no contest: a numerator bounded away from zero divided by something shrinking to zero grows without bound in magnitude, so the size of the limit is already determined, with only the sign, and hence whether the two-sided limit is plus or minus infinity or non-existent, left to check.

questions.q: Explain why direct substitution is guaranteed to work for every polynomial, and why it is therefore not a general method that may be tried on an arbitrary function.
questions.concept: Substitution is a consequence of continuity, not a definition of the limit.
questions.why: A full answer derives it: lim x = a and lim c = c are the basic limits, and repeated use of the product, constant-multiple and sum laws builds any polynomial from these, so its limit at a equals its value at a. That is the statement that polynomials are continuous everywhere. It must then say that substitution is legitimate only where continuity has been established, so for a rational function it needs a non-zero denominator at a, and for a piecewise or oscillating function it can fail outright; substituting into f(x) = |x|/x at 0, or into a function with a jump, gives either nonsense or the wrong number.

questions.q: Explain why L'Hopital's Rule is not a disguised form of the quotient rule, and why the indeterminate form has to be re-checked before every single application.
questions.concept: The mechanism of L'Hopital (local linear approximation of numerator and denominator) versus the derivative of a quotient.
questions.why: A full answer distinguishes the objects: the quotient rule computes the derivative of f/g and yields (f'g - fg')/g^2, which is a different function altogether, whereas L'Hopital replaces the ratio f/g by the ratio f'/g' of the separate derivatives. The mechanism should be given: when f(a) = g(a) = 0, near a we have f(x) approximately f'(a)(x - a) and g(x) approximately g'(a)(x - a), so the common factor (x - a) cancels and the ratio tends to f'(a)/g'(a). It must then state that this cancellation argument only exists while both functions vanish (or both blow up), so after one differentiation the new quotient must be substituted into again; if it is no longer 0/0 or infinity/infinity, differentiating once more changes the value and gives a wrong answer, as with lim(x to 0) (cos x)/(x + 1).
