It also covers the meaning of the minus sign in Faraday's law, the idea that electrostatic energy is stored in the field itself with density one-half epsilon-nought E squared, why the factor of one half appears in the capacitor energy, and what a dielectric does to capacitance, field and breakdown. No lengthy calculation is required; every question asks what a quantity means, why a relation holds, or what would go wrong without it.

questions.q: A torch cell reads 1.50 V on a voltmeter with nothing else connected, and 1.20 V when it is lighting a bulb. What has become of the missing 0.30 V?
options: The cell's emf has genuinely dropped to 1.20 V because chemical energy is being consumed
The voltmeter loads the circuit and under-reads by 0.30 V once current flows
It is the potential drop Ir across the cell's own internal resistance, dissipated inside the cell
It is stored in the magnetic field of the current-carrying wires and returns when the switch opens
questions.concept: Terminal p.d. versus emf: V = epsilon - Ir, and the physical meaning of the lost volts.
questions.why: The emf is fixed by the cell's chemistry; once current I flows, a p.d. Ir appears across the internal resistance r and is dissipated as heat inside the cell, so only epsilon - Ir is available at the terminals.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to treat electromotive force as a kind of force acting on charges?
options: Because emf is energy supplied per unit charge, measured in joules per coulomb, not in newtons
Because emf acts only on the ions inside the cell, whereas force acts on the electrons in the wire
Because emf is a rate of energy transfer, so it is a power and is measured in watts
Because emf is defined only for alternating sources, while force is defined for steady ones
questions.concept: Definition and unit of emf: work done per unit charge, unit volt = J/C, dimension M L^2 T^-3 I^-1.
questions.why: Emf is defined as W/Q, so its unit is the volt (one joule per coulomb) and its dimension is M L^2 T^-3 I^-1 — a quantity of energy per charge, which is not a force at all.

questions.q: In Faraday's law written as emf = -N dPhi/dt, what does the minus sign assert?
options: That the induced emf is always smaller than the applied emf that produced the flux
That the induced emf is negative energy, so the coil absorbs rather than supplies power
That flux must be decreasing for an emf to be induced at all
That the induced emf drives a current whose own flux opposes the change that created it
questions.concept: The sign in Faraday's law is Lenz's law: it fixes direction, not magnitude.
questions.why: The minus sign encodes Lenz's law — the induced current is directed so that its magnetic effect opposes the change in flux, which is what makes induction consistent with energy conservation; it says nothing about the size of the emf.

questions.q: A conducting rod slides on frictionless rails through a field B perpendicular to the plane. Which statement describes what actually separates charge in the rod?
options: The changing flux creates a static charge imbalance directly, without any force acting on carriers
Each free charge q moves with the rod at speed v, so it feels a magnetic force qvB along the rod that pushes carriers towards one end
Friction between the rod and the rails strips electrons and deposits them at one end
The magnetic field magnetises the metal, and the resulting poles attract electrons to one end
questions.concept: Microscopic origin of motional emf: the Lorentz force qvB on carriers carried along by the moving conductor.
questions.why: Because the carriers travel with the rod at v, each experiences F = qvB directed along the rod; the work per unit charge in moving a carrier the length l is Bvl, which is exactly the motional emf.

questions.q: The expression one-half epsilon-nought E squared is said to be the energy stored per unit volume in an electric field. What is the physical claim being made?
options: That the energy is located in the field itself, so a region of empty space carrying a field holds energy
That energy resides only on the surfaces of the plates, and the expression is a bookkeeping convenience
That the energy belongs to the dielectric molecules, so the expression is zero in a vacuum
That the energy is carried by the moving electrons in the connecting wires while the capacitor charges
questions.concept: Energy density of the electric field: energy resides in the field, and persists in vacuum.
questions.why: The deck's point is that even in space devoid of matter the energy persists: the field itself is the store, with density one-half epsilon-nought E squared, and multiplying by the volume Ad recovers the capacitor's total energy.

questions.q: Why does the energy stored in a capacitor come out as one-half QV rather than QV?
options: Because half the charge always leaks back through the dielectric while the capacitor is charging
Because only half of the plate area carries charge at any instant
Because the field between the plates occupies only half the volume Ad
Because the p.d. rises from zero to V as charge is added, so each element of charge is moved through an average p.d. of V/2
questions.concept: Why the factor of one half appears in U = QV/2 = CV^2/2: the p.d. is not constant during charging.
questions.why: Charging is progressive: the first charge crosses at almost no p.d. and the last at V, so the mean p.d. is V/2 and the work is QV/2. QV would be the work only if the p.d. were held at V throughout.

questions.q: Faraday found that filling the gap between capacitor plates with an insulator multiplies the capacitance by a factor K. What does a larger K mean physically for the capacitor?
options: The insulator conducts a little, so charge leaks across and the plates hold more of it
The dielectric partly cancels the field of the plate charge, so the same charge produces a smaller p.d. and Q/V is larger
The dielectric increases the plate separation d, which raises C because C is proportional to d
The dielectric raises the emf of the source that charges it, so more charge is driven onto the plates
questions.concept: Dielectric constant K: the polarised dielectric reduces the net field for a given charge, so C = K epsilon-nought A/d.
questions.why: The dielectric polarises and its bound surface charge opposes the field of the free charge; the net field, and therefore V = Ed, is reduced for the same Q, so C = Q/V rises by the factor K. A dielectric that conducted would destroy the capacitor, not improve it.

questions.q: Two identical capacitors are to store the largest possible energy from one supply of fixed potential difference V. Why does the parallel arrangement win?
options: Because in parallel each capacitor receives only half the voltage, and halving V doubles the stored energy
Because in series the same charge passes through both, and shared charge always means shared energy
Because the equivalent capacitance in parallel is the sum, which is larger than any series combination, and at fixed V the energy CV^2/2 grows with C
Because in parallel the plate separation is effectively halved, which raises the field between the plates
questions.concept: Series versus parallel combination and the dependence of stored energy on C at fixed V.
questions.why: Parallel capacitances add, giving the largest obtainable C_eq, and both capacitors sit at the full supply voltage; since U = CV^2/2 at fixed V, the largest C stores the most energy. In series C_eq is smaller than the smallest member and each capacitor gets only part of V.

questions.q: Explain why the graph of terminal p.d. V against current I for a real cell is a straight line with a negative gradient, and why the intercept on the V axis is the emf.
questions.concept: The V-I characteristic of a source: V = epsilon - rI as the equation of a straight line, and what each feature of the line corresponds to physically.
questions.why: A full answer states that the loop equation epsilon = V + Ir rearranges to V = epsilon - rI, which has the form y = c + mx with V as y and I as x. Because r is a constant property of the cell, the line is straight; because the internal drop Ir grows with current, the gradient is -r (negative, and r is its magnitude). Extrapolating to I = 0 removes the internal drop entirely, so the V-axis intercept is the open-circuit terminal p.d., which equals the emf. It should add that in practice the cell drains as readings are taken, so the cell is disconnected between readings to keep the line straight.

questions.q: Explain why a rod sliding along the direction of the magnetic field lines produces no motional emf, while the same rod sliding perpendicular to them does.
questions.concept: The geometry of motional emf: the cross-product nature of qv x B and the requirement that the enclosed flux actually change.
questions.why: A full answer works from the Lorentz force: the force on a carrier is q v x B, which vanishes when v is parallel to B, so no carrier is pushed along the rod and no charge separates, giving zero emf. When v is perpendicular to B, the force qvB acts along the rod and drives carriers to one end until an electrostatic field balances it, giving emf = Bvl. Equivalently, in flux language Phi = Blx changes only when the motion sweeps out area across the field lines; motion along B sweeps out no additional flux, so dPhi/dt = 0.

questions.q: Explain why the energy of a charged capacitor can legitimately be said to reside in the empty space between the plates rather than on the plates themselves.
questions.concept: Field energy and energy density: locating electrostatic energy in the field, and the consistency check between one-half epsilon-nought E squared times Ad and CV^2/2.
questions.why: A full answer notes that between parallel plates the field is essentially uniform and outside it is essentially zero, so assigning a uniform density u = one-half epsilon-nought E squared to the gap and zero elsewhere reproduces the total: u times the volume Ad equals one-half epsilon-nought E squared A d, and substituting E = V/d and C = epsilon-nought A/d turns this into CV^2/2, the energy the battery actually supplied. Because the two routes agree for any A, d and V, the field-energy description is not merely bookkeeping. It should add that this makes energy present in a vacuum, which is what allows electromagnetic energy to travel where no charges are.

questions.q: Explain why a defibrillator can deliver a very high power to a patient even though the battery charging its capacitor supplies only a modest power.
questions.concept: Energy versus power in capacitor storage and discharge: the capacitor as a slow-fill, fast-empty energy reservoir.
questions.why: A full answer separates energy from power. The battery transfers energy slowly over seconds, storing U = CV^2/2 in the capacitor by separating charge, so the charging power U/t_charge is small. Closing the switch discharges part of that stored energy through the paddles in a few milliseconds, and power is energy divided by time, so the same joules delivered over a thousand times shorter interval give a thousand times larger power. Nothing creates energy: the capacitor only redistributes in time what the battery supplied, converting chemical energy to electrostatic potential energy and back.

checks.topic: Computational approaches to problem solving, treated conceptually. This session covers what a computational approach is and the three factors (clear definition, computability, data requirements) that decide whether one can be used; the mechanism and cost of each of the eleven named approaches — problem recognition, backtracking, data mining, performance testing, pipelining, visualisation, brute force, divide and conquer, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming and hypothesis testing. The emphasis is on why each approach works, what it costs, and the conditions under which it fails: the divide-and-conquer recombination condition, the greedy algorithm's lack of an optimality guarantee against dynamic programming's guarantee, and the meaning of significance level and p-value in the accept/reject rule. It does not ask for traces or worked arithmetic; that is Saturday.

questions.q: The lesson calls brute force 'simple and consistent, but very slow'. What makes it consistent?
options: It goes through every possible choice, so any solution present in that space will be reached
It uses recursion to move systematically from one problem state to the next until the search is exhausted
It applies the best available option at each stage, so no stage can be worse than the last
It saves the result of each choice it has already evaluated, so no choice is tried twice
questions.concept: Brute force: exhaustive enumeration is the source of its reliability and simultaneously the source of its cost.
questions.why: Brute force relies solely on computing power, trying every possibility rather than improving efficiency with advanced techniques; because nothing is skipped, a solution present in the search space is certain to be found — and because nothing is skipped, the work grows with the size of that space.

questions.q: A student splits a scheduling problem into four sub-problems, solves each, and finds the combined solution takes longer to assemble than solving the original problem directly would have. What has gone wrong with the divide and conquer application?
options: The four sub-problems were not of equal size, so their partial solutions cannot be merged into one schedule
The recombination step is not simpler than the original problem, so the split buys nothing
The sub-problems do not overlap, so no intermediate result could be reused
The sub-problems were solved in parallel rather than each feeding into the next
questions.concept: The condition for divide and conquer: the parts must be simpler than the whole AND recombining them must cost less than solving the original directly.
questions.why: Divide and conquer only works if the small easier parts are genuinely simpler than the complex part and the cost of combining their solutions is lower than solving the original outright; when assembly is the expensive step, the decomposition has added work instead of removing it.

questions.q: Both greedy algorithms and dynamic programming work stage by stage, yet only dynamic programming guarantees an optimal solution when one exists. Why?
options: Dynamic programming examines every possible candidate exhaustively, whereas a greedy algorithm examines only a small sample of them
Greedy uses recursion and therefore loses information when the recursion unwinds
Greedy fixes its choice at each stage, while dynamic programming saves sub-problem solutions and compares combinations
Dynamic programming is applied only to problems that have exactly one solution, so optimality is automatic
questions.concept: Greedy irrevocability vs dynamic programming's stored sub-problem solutions — the actual source of the optimality guarantee.
questions.why: The greedy algorithm applies the best possible solution at each stage and moves on, so a locally attractive choice can close off a better overall completion with no way back; dynamic programming breaks the problem into sub-problems and saves their solutions, so the combinations are available for comparison and, provided a solution exists, an optimal one can be found.

questions.q: What distinguishes pipelining from the other decomposition approaches covered this week?
options: The task is broken into sub-problems whose solutions are stored so they need not be recomputed
The task is broken into parts that are each solved independently and then combined into the whole
The task is broken into candidate solutions that are generated and tested one after another until one of them is accepted
The task is split into a series of subtasks run by different processes, each result feeding the next
questions.concept: Pipelining as a serial dependency chain, as opposed to independent decomposition (divide and conquer) or stored reuse (dynamic programming).
questions.why: Pipelining divides a task into a series of subtasks where each subtask leads to the next; each subtask runs in a different process and the result of one feeds the next, repeatedly, until the whole task is completed. The order is load-bearing, which is exactly what independent decomposition lacks.

questions.q: In backtracking, what does the algorithm do when it reaches a final state?
options: It checks whether the state is accepted or rejected, then retreats to a previous state for untried options
It records the value reached at that state so that the same state need never be evaluated a second time later
It compares that state against all remaining states and keeps whichever scores highest
It abandons the current search entirely and begins again from a different starting state
questions.concept: The backtracking cycle: decide, reach a final state, accept or reject, retreat to the last decision point and take an unconsidered option.
questions.why: At every step possible options are considered and a decision made; on reaching a final state the algorithm checks acceptance or rejection and then backtracks to a previous state to try other unconsidered options. Recording values for reuse is dynamic programming, not backtracking.

questions.q: A test is run at a significance level of 0.05. What does that number mean?
options: There is a 5% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 5% risk of concluding that something exists when it does not exist
At least 5% of the collected data must contradict the null hypothesis before it can be rejected
The p-value produced by the data will fall within 5% of its true value
questions.concept: Significance level as the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis — a risk fixed in advance, not a statement about the data or about the null hypothesis being true.
questions.why: The significance level is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact true, so 0.05 indicates a 5% risk of concluding that something exists when it does not. The probability of the null hypothesis being true is what the p-value speaks to, and that comes from the data, not from the chosen level.

questions.q: A team is deciding whether a problem can be tackled computationally at all. Which consideration belongs to the factor 'the problem needs to be computable'?
options: Whether the current situation, the end goal, the route to it and the possible obstacles have been identified
Whether the problem can be grouped as a specific type of problem already understood
Whether the required calculations are possible, given processing times and capacity
Whether the data types the problem needs and the storage capacity for them are available
questions.concept: Separating the three pre-conditions: clearly defined (situation, goal, route, obstacles), computable (calculations feasible in time and capacity), data requirements (types and storage).
questions.why: Computability here is specifically about whether the required calculations can be performed at all given processing time and capacity. Identifying situation, goal and obstacles is the 'clearly defined' factor, data types and storage is the 'data requirements' factor, and grouping the problem by type belongs to problem recognition.

questions.q: Visualisation is listed as a computational approach even though the lesson says it helps humans rather than computers. On what does its usefulness rest?
options: It lowers the number of calculations a machine has to perform to reach the same answer
It restates the problem in a graphical form, such as a graph or a tree, that a computer can then solve automatically
It provides a set of test scenarios against which a program's output can be measured
People retain information better as an image than as text, so the problem becomes easier to grasp
questions.concept: Visualisation as a cognitive aid to the human solver, not a computational saving — which is why the beneficiary test separates it from data mining and performance testing.
questions.why: Visualisation uses diagrams, graphs and images to illustrate what a problem entails and how to approach its solution, and it works on the knowledge that people process and retain information better in image form than in text; the gain is in human understanding, not in machine work.

questions.q: Explain why a greedy algorithm can return a non-optimal answer even though it selects the best available option at every single stage.
questions.concept: Local optimality does not compose into global optimality when an early choice constrains what remains available.
questions.why: A full answer must say that the greedy algorithm applies the best possible solution at each stage and then moves on without revisiting that decision; the choice is evaluated only against what looks best at that moment, not against what it leaves possible afterwards. It must then give the mechanism: taking the locally best option can consume or block resources needed for a better overall completion, and because there is no backtracking or stored alternative the algorithm can never recover. It should close by noting that on problems where the local choice provably cannot block a better completion the greedy solution is optimal, and there it is simple and highly efficient.

questions.q: Explain why dynamic programming's saving of sub-problem solutions is what converts it from mere decomposition into an approach that guarantees an optimal solution.
questions.concept: Storage of sub-problem solutions is the mechanism behind both the efficiency and the optimality guarantee — decomposition alone gives neither.
questions.why: A full answer must state that dynamic programming breaks a problem into sub-problems and saves the solutions so the same result is never computed twice, and that this store is what makes exhaustive comparison of combinations affordable: without it, re-deriving the same sub-problem repeatedly makes the comparison too expensive to carry out. It should then say that because every sub-problem's best solution is available, the best combination for the whole can be identified, so provided a solution exists an optimal one can be found — and note that this is why dynamic programming is used mostly for optimization problems, where a minimum or maximum is required.

questions.q: Explain why a p-value higher than the significance level leads to accepting the null hypothesis, and why doing so does not establish that no effect exists.
questions.concept: The accept/reject rule as a comparison of computed evidence against a pre-set risk threshold, and the asymmetry between insufficient evidence and proof of absence.
questions.why: A full answer must define the p-value as a number between 0 and 1 describing how likely it is that the null hypothesis is true, with a smaller value giving stronger evidence to reject it, and the significance level as the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, fixed in advance. It must then give the rule: p less than or equal to the significance level means reject, p higher means accept — because a high p-value means the data are not unlikely under the null hypothesis, so the pre-agreed threshold of evidence has not been met. Finally it must say that failing to meet that threshold means the evidence is not enough, which is not the same as showing there is nothing to find; a larger or better-designed study could still reject the same null hypothesis.

questions.q: Explain why backtracking is a cheaper way of examining more than one possible solution than brute force is, even though both may end up considering many candidates.
questions.concept: Backtracking abandons a partial candidate as soon as its state is rejected and resumes from the last decision point; brute force has no notion of a partial candidate.
questions.why: A full answer must say that brute force goes through all possible complete choices, relying solely on computing power, with no way to tell that a candidate is doomed before it is finished. It must then give the backtracking mechanism: options are considered step by step, and on reaching a state that is rejected the algorithm returns to a previous state and takes an option not yet considered, so every complete candidate sharing that rejected prefix is dropped in one move. The maze example makes it concrete — a dead end is recognised at the leaf and the search resumes from the last junction rather than re-walking whole routes. It should note the cost is not free: recursion carries the state needed to retreat, and in the worst case, where nothing can be rejected early, backtracking degenerates into the same exhaustive search as brute force.

checks.topic: The same Week 3 limit material worked as problems: reading a limit, substituting first, and classifying what comes back as a number, as a non-zero over zero, or as an indeterminate 0/0 or infinity/infinity. Choosing among direct substitution, factorization and cancellation, conjugate rationalization for radicals, clearing a compound fraction, dividing by the highest power for limits at infinity, and L'Hopital's Rule, then executing the chosen route accurately. Checking a finished answer for plausibility, including sign analysis of one-sided infinite limits. Diagnosing two standard wrong routes: applying L'Hopital to a quotient that was never indeterminate, and using the quotient rule in place of L'Hopital.

questions.q: For lim(x to 4) (sqrt(x) - 2)/(x - 4), substitution gives 0/0. What is the correct first move?
options: Divide the numerator and the denominator by x, the highest power appearing in the expression.
Multiply the numerator and the denominator by sqrt(x) + 2.
Report 0/0 as the value of the limit, since that is what substitution returns.
Factor x - 4 as (x - 2)(x + 2) and cancel the x - 2 against the numerator.
questions.concept: Recognising a radical 0/0 and selecting conjugate rationalization over the other routes.
questions.why: The conjugate turns (sqrt(x) - 2)(sqrt(x) + 2) into x - 4, which cancels the denominator and leaves 1/(sqrt(x) + 2), giving 1/4 by substitution. Option d misfactors x - 4, which is not a difference of squares in x.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x to 3) (x^2 - 9)/(x^2 - 4x + 3).
questions.concept: Factorization and cancellation on a 0/0 rational limit, then substitution into the reduced form.
questions.why: Both parts factor with a common (x - 3): (x - 3)(x + 3) over (x - 3)(x - 1) reduces to (x + 3)/(x - 1), which at x = 3 gives 6/2 = 3.

questions.q: A student writes: lim(x to 0) (cos x)/(x + 1) = lim(x to 0) (-sin x)/1 = 0. What is the fault?
options: The quotient was not indeterminate, since substitution gives 1/1, so L'Hopital does not apply and the true limit is 1.
The derivative of cos x is sin x rather than -sin x, so the method was right and only the differentiation was wrong.
L'Hopital's Rule is only valid for limits as x tends to infinity, never at a finite point.
The quotient rule should have been used, giving (-sin x (x + 1) - cos x)/(x + 1)^2 before taking the limit.
questions.concept: Verifying the indeterminate form before invoking L'Hopital; an unlicensed application changes the answer.
questions.why: Substituting x = 0 gives cos 0 / (0 + 1) = 1, a perfectly determinate value, so the rule's hypothesis fails and its conclusion, 0, is simply a different number from the correct limit 1.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x to infinity) (2x^2 + 3)/(5x^2 - x).
options: infinity
questions.concept: Limits at infinity for rational functions: divide by the highest power in the denominator.
questions.why: Dividing top and bottom by x^2 gives (2 + 3/x^2)/(5 - 1/x), and the reciprocal-power terms vanish, leaving 2/5 as the ratio of leading coefficients.

questions.q: Asked for lim(x to 0) (sin 3x)/(5x) by L'Hopital, a student writes [3cos(3x)(5x) - 5 sin(3x)]/(5x)^2. What has gone wrong and what is the right result?
options: The derivative of sin 3x is wrong; it should be cos 3x, after which the working is sound.
L'Hopital cannot be used at all here, because sin 3x is not a polynomial.
Nothing is wrong; simplifying that expression and taking the limit does return the correct value 3/5.
The quotient rule has been applied to the whole fraction, whereas L'Hopital differentiates numerator and denominator separately, giving 3cos(3x)/5 and hence 3/5.
questions.concept: Distinguishing L'Hopital's f'/g' from the derivative of a quotient (f'g - fg')/g^2.
questions.why: The tell-tale g^2 in the denominator shows the quotient rule was used; L'Hopital requires the separate derivatives 3cos(3x) and 5, whose ratio tends to 3/5.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x to 1) ((1/x) - 1)/(x - 1).
options: The limit does not exist.
questions.concept: Clearing a compound fraction before cancelling, on a 0/0 form.
questions.why: Writing the numerator over a common denominator gives (1 - x)/x, so the expression is (1 - x)/[x(x - 1)] = -1/x for x not equal to 1, whose limit at 1 is -1.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x to 2 from the right) 1/(x - 2), and identify the check that settles it.
options: 0, because the denominator becomes small and dividing by a small number makes the result small.
It is indeterminate, being of the form 1/0, so L'Hopital's Rule must be applied.
Plus infinity, because the numerator holds at 1 while the denominator tends to 0 through positive values.
Minus infinity, because the denominator x - 2 is negative for x just to the right of 2.
questions.concept: Non-zero over zero is not indeterminate; the sign of the denominator on the approach side fixes the sign of the infinity.
questions.why: For x > 2 the quantity x - 2 is a small positive number, so its reciprocal grows without bound in the positive direction; a finite answer would signal a structural mistake.

questions.q: Applying L'Hopital's Rule as many times as the form requires, lim(x to 0) (1 - cos x)/x^2 equals
options: The limit does not exist.
questions.concept: Repeated application of L'Hopital, with the form re-checked between applications.
questions.why: The first application gives sin x / (2x), still 0/0, and the second gives cos x / 2, which is determinate and equals 1/2 at x = 0.

questions.q: Explain why substituting the value first is never a wasted step, even when you can already see the limit will come out indeterminate.
questions.concept: Substitution as the diagnostic that classifies the problem and licenses every later technique.
questions.why: A full answer says that substitution is not an attempt at the answer but the classification step: it sorts the problem into a finite value (done, by continuity), a non-zero over zero (an infinite limit, whose sign is then read off from each side), or 0/0 and infinity/infinity (indeterminate, needing algebra or L'Hopital). It must state that no later technique is licensed until this classification is made: L'Hopital's hypothesis is exactly that the substituted form is indeterminate, and cancelling or rationalizing is pointless work when substitution already returns a number. It should add that the same check must be repeated after each application of L'Hopital, since the form can stop being indeterminate mid-problem.

questions.q: Explain why factorization and L'Hopital's Rule return the same value for lim(x to 2) (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2), even though the two routes manipulate the expression in quite different ways.
questions.concept: Both routes remove the same vanishing factor; L'Hopital does it via local linear approximation.
questions.why: A full answer identifies the shared mechanism: the 0/0 arises because a factor (x - 2) is present in both numerator and denominator, and both methods eliminate exactly that factor. Factorization does it explicitly, writing (x + 2)(x - 2)/(x - 2) = x + 2 for x not equal to 2, giving 4. L'Hopital does it implicitly: near 2 the numerator behaves like its derivative times (x - 2), that is 4(x - 2), and the denominator like 1 times (x - 2), so the ratio of the derivatives 2x/1 evaluated at 2 gives the same 4. The answer should note that the agreement is not a coincidence but the content of the rule, and that the factorization route stays available even where the functions are not differentiable, while L'Hopital extends to cases such as sin x / x that will not factor.

questions.q: Explain why multiplying by the conjugate converts a 0/0 limit involving a square root into one that substitution can finish.
questions.concept: The conjugate uses the difference-of-squares identity to move the vanishing factor out of the radical and into a cancellable polynomial factor.
questions.why: A full answer explains that (sqrt(u) - c)(sqrt(u) + c) = u - c^2, so the multiplication removes the radical from the part that is vanishing and produces a plain polynomial factor identical to the one in the denominator. That factor is non-zero for every x in the punctured neighbourhood, so it may be cancelled, and what is left, such as 1/(sqrt(x) + 2), has a non-zero denominator at the target point and is therefore continuous there, which is what makes substitution legal. It must add that the conjugate is deliberately placed on the side carrying the radical, and that multiplying above and below by the same non-zero quantity leaves the function unchanged away from the point, so the limit is untouched.

questions.q: Explain why an answer of 0 for lim(x to 2 from the right) 1/(x - 2) is a structural error rather than an arithmetic slip, and what checking the sign of the denominator from each side reveals.
questions.concept: Reading non-zero over zero correctly, and using one-sided sign analysis to check an infinite limit.
questions.why: A full answer says the error is in classification: a numerator with a non-zero limit over a denominator tending to zero produces a quotient whose magnitude grows without bound, so any finite answer, and 0 in particular, has the behaviour exactly backwards; the student has confused a small denominator with a small quotient. The check is to take the sign of x - 2 on the approach side: for x slightly greater than 2 it is a small positive number, so 1/(x - 2) tends to plus infinity, while for x slightly less than 2 it is small and negative, so the left-hand limit is minus infinity. It should conclude that because the two one-sided limits disagree in sign, the two-sided limit at 2 does not exist and x = 2 is an infinite discontinuity, a vertical asymptote, not a removable one.

checks.topic: Week 3 of General Physics II worked as problems: setting up and solving circuit questions with internal resistance using epsilon = I(R + r) and V = epsilon - Ir, extracting emf and internal resistance from a V-I graph, computing motional emf from Bvl and the induced current, force and power that follow, and applying Faraday's law with N turns to a changing flux. It also covers capacitor numerical work: C = K epsilon-nought A/d, V = Ed, U = CV^2/2 = Q^2/2C, and energy density one-half epsilon E squared multiplied by the volume Ad. Several questions ask you to diagnose a wrong route rather than produce a number, and to check an answer by units or by a second independent relation. Take epsilon-nought = 8.85 x 10^-12 F/m.

questions.q: A cell of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 ohm is connected to a 3.0 ohm resistor. What is the potential difference across the 3.0 ohm resistor?
questions.concept: Setting up a single-loop circuit: I = epsilon/(R + r), then V = IR = epsilon - Ir.
questions.why: I = 9.0/(3.0 + 1.5) = 2.0 A, so the p.d. across the external resistor is IR = 2.0 x 3.0 = 6.0 V, which also equals epsilon - Ir = 9.0 - 3.0.

questions.q: Solving the same circuit, a student writes I = epsilon/R and ignores r entirely. What is the effect on the answers?
options: The current is unchanged but the terminal p.d. comes out too small
Both the current and the terminal p.d. come out too small
The current comes out too small, and the terminal p.d. then exceeds the emf
The current comes out too large, and the terminal p.d. is wrongly reported as equal to the emf
questions.concept: Diagnosing the commonest circuit error: omitting internal resistance from the total resistance of the loop.
questions.why: Dividing by R alone rather than R + r gives a current larger than the true value, and since IR is then taken as the whole of epsilon there are no lost volts left, so the terminal p.d. is wrongly equal to the emf.

questions.q: A student cannot remember the motional-emf formula and wants to settle it by units. Which of these combinations has the units of volts?
options: Bvl
Bv/l
Bl/v
Bv/l squared
questions.concept: Using dimensional checking to recover or verify a formula: 1 T = 1 V s / m^2.
questions.why: One tesla is one weber per square metre, i.e. one volt-second per square metre, so B v l has units (V s m^-2)(m s^-1)(m) = V. The other combinations are short by one or two powers of length and cannot be a potential difference.

questions.q: A dielectric of constant K = 2.5 fills the gap of a capacitor in which the field is 400 V/m. What is the energy stored per unit volume?
questions.concept: Energy density with a dielectric present: u = one-half K epsilon-nought E squared, in joules per cubic metre.

questions.q: A 3.0 microfarad capacitor carries a charge of 6.0 microcoulombs. The energy stored is
questions.concept: Choosing the right form of the capacitor energy expression when Q and C are given rather than V.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m^2 lies perpendicular to a magnetic field that is increasing steadily at 0.50 T/s. The magnitude of the induced emf is
questions.concept: Applying Faraday's law when the area is fixed and B changes: emf = N A dB/dt.
questions.why: Phi = BA with A constant, so the magnitude of the emf is N A dB/dt = 100 x 0.020 x 0.50 = 1.0 V.

questions.q: Asked for the energy stored in a 4.7 microfarad capacitor charged to 50 V, a student reports 1.2 x 10^-4 J instead of the correct 5.9 x 10^-3 J. What did the student do?
options: Used Q^2/2C with the charge taken as CV^2 instead of CV
Divided by 2 twice, once in the formula and once when converting microfarads
Used CV/2 instead of CV^2/2, i.e. failed to square the voltage
Used the field-energy formula one-half epsilon-nought E squared instead of the capacitor formula
questions.concept: Diagnosing a wrong route from the size of the answer: tracking which factor of V was dropped.
questions.why: 0.5 x 4.7 x 10^-6 x 50 = 1.18 x 10^-4 J, exactly the reported figure, so the voltage was used to the first power; the ratio of wrong to right answer is 1/50, which is the missing factor of V.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.80 m slides at 5.0 m/s on rails in a field of 0.25 T perpendicular to the plane; the circuit has a total resistance of 0.50 ohm. What mechanical power must be supplied to keep the rod moving at constant speed?
questions.concept: Chaining motional emf to current, force and power, and checking with the energy balance Fv = I^2 R.
questions.why: emf = Bvl = 0.25 x 5.0 x 0.80 = 1.0 V, so I = 1.0/0.50 = 2.0 A and the dissipated power is I^2 R = 4.0 x 0.50 = 2.0 W; the same follows from F = BIl = 0.40 N and P = Fv = 2.0 W.

questions.q: Explain why, in a problem giving emf, internal resistance and external resistance, you must add r to R before dividing into the emf, and show with a numerical illustration how large the error is if you do not.
questions.concept: Why the loop equation uses the total resistance: the internal resistance is part of the same series path the current must traverse.
questions.why: A full answer says the current is the same everywhere in a single loop, and the charge that passes through R must also pass through the cell's own resistance r, so the emf is shared between the two drops: epsilon = IR + Ir = I(R + r). Dividing by R alone treats the cell as ideal. It must supply a worked illustration, for example epsilon = 6.0 V, R = 2.0 ohm, r = 1.0 ohm: the correct I = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A with V = 4.0 V, whereas ignoring r gives I = 3.0 A and V = 6.0 V, a fifty per cent error in current. It should note that the error grows as R approaches r, and is negligible only when R is much larger than r.

questions.q: Explain why computing a capacitor's stored energy as one-half epsilon-nought E squared times Ad must give the same number as one-half CV squared, and why this makes a good check on a numerical answer.
questions.concept: Cross-checking a result by two independent relations, using V = Ed and C = epsilon-nought A/d to show the two routes are algebraically identical.
questions.why: A full answer substitutes: with V = Ed and C = epsilon-nought A/d, one-half CV^2 = one-half (epsilon-nought A/d)(Ed)^2 = one-half epsilon-nought E^2 (Ad), so the two expressions are the same quantity written with different variables. It should say that because the two routes use different given data (E, A, d in one case; C, V in the other), an arithmetic slip or a units slip in one route will almost never be repeated in the other, so agreement to two or three significant figures is strong evidence the answer is right. A worked check should be shown, for example A = 0.02 m^2, d = 0.005 m, E = 200 N/C giving C = 3.54 x 10^-11 F, V = 1.0 V and U = 1.77 x 10^-11 J by both routes.

questions.q: Explain why an answer of '1.77 x 10^-7 J' for the quantity one-half epsilon-nought E squared should be rejected on sight, and what the correct statement of that result is.
questions.concept: Distinguishing total energy from energy density by dimensions, and the discipline of carrying units through a calculation.
questions.why: A full answer performs the unit check: epsilon-nought is in farads per metre and E in volts per metre, so epsilon-nought E^2 has units F V^2 m^-3, and since a farad-volt-squared is a joule the result is joules per cubic metre, an energy density, not an energy. It must state that the correct answer is 1.77 x 10^-7 J/m^3 and that joules are obtained only after multiplying by the volume between the plates Ad; for A = 0.02 m^2 and d = 0.005 m that volume is 1.0 x 10^-4 m^3, giving U = 1.77 x 10^-11 J. It should note that this is exactly the slip on the lecture slide.

questions.q: Explain why, for a rod being pulled at constant speed along rails, the mechanical power you supply comes out equal to the electrical power I squared R dissipated in the circuit, and why this equality is a legitimate check on a motional-emf answer.
questions.concept: Energy conservation in motional emf: the retarding force BIl on the induced current is what the applied force must balance, so mechanical input equals electrical output.
questions.why: A full answer notes that the induced current I in the rod sits in the field B, so the rod experiences a force BIl opposing its motion (Lenz's law); at constant speed the applied force must equal this, so the mechanical power is Fv = BIlv. Substituting emf = Bvl gives Fv = I x emf = I x IR = I^2 R, the dissipated electrical power. Since no energy is stored in the rod at constant speed, the two must be equal, and computing both from separately derived quantities (F and v on one side, I and R on the other) catches an error in the emf, the current or the force. A numerical illustration such as B = 0.25 T, l = 0.80 m, v = 5.0 m/s, R = 0.50 ohm giving 2.0 W by both routes completes it.

checks.topic: The same Week 3 computational approaches, treated as practice. This session applies them to the concrete problems the lessons name: counting the search space of the four-digit padlock under brute force, tracing Merge sort on a small set as a divide and conquer algorithm, running the greedy activity-selection example with start times 2, 4, 1, 6, 9, 6 and end times 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 10, and converting a naive recursive Fibonacci into a dynamic programming solution. It also asks which named approach fits a described situation, how to lay out a pipelined calculation, and how to diagnose a solution that is wrong or wastefully slow, including the food-delivery routing case study. Definitions are assumed known from Wednesday; here they must be executed.

questions.q: A padlock has four digit wheels, each showing 0 to 9, and the combination has been forgotten. How many combinations must a brute force attack be prepared to try in the worst case?
questions.concept: Sizing the search space a brute force approach must enumerate: independent positions multiply, and repeated values are allowed.
questions.why: Each of the four wheels is set independently to one of ten values, so the space is 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000. It is not 4 x 10 because the wheels combine rather than add, not 5,040 because digits may repeat so this is not a permutation of distinct digits, and not 9,999 because 0000 is itself a valid combination.

questions.q: Merge sort is used to arrange 2, 8, 4, 9, 3 in descending order. The list is split into [2, 8] and [4, 9, 3]. What are the two halves immediately before the final merge?
options: [9, 8, 4, 3, 2] and an empty list
questions.concept: Tracing Merge sort: each half is recursively sorted into the target order before the single final merge, and the target order here is descending.
questions.why: Each half is sorted in the order being asked for, which is descending, so [2, 8] becomes [8, 2] and [4, 9, 3] becomes [9, 4, 3]. Sorting the halves ascending would produce the wrong final order, and the fully sorted list is the output of the final merge, not its input.

questions.q: Six activities have start times 2, 4, 1, 6, 9, 6 and end times 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 10 respectively, and no two may be worked on at once. What is the maximum number of activities that can be performed?
questions.concept: Executing the greedy activity-selection procedure on the lesson's own data and checking each candidate for overlap.
questions.why: Taking the compatible activity that finishes earliest each time gives (2,3), then (4,5), then (6,8), then (9,10) — four activities. Activity (1,7) overlaps (2,3) and (4,5), and (6,10) overlaps (9,10), so neither can be added.

questions.q: For the activity-selection problem, which greedy selection rule can be relied on to produce the maximum number of activities?
options: Repeatedly take the compatible activity that has the earliest start time among those remaining
Repeatedly take the compatible activity with the latest start time
Repeatedly take the compatible activity with the shortest duration
Repeatedly take the compatible activity with the earliest finishing time
questions.concept: Which local criterion is actually safe in a greedy algorithm — the criterion, not the greediness, is what makes the answer optimal.
questions.why: Finishing earliest leaves the largest possible remainder of the timeline free, so it can never rule out a better completion; on this data it yields four activities, whereas taking the earliest start first locks in (1,7) and yields only two. Shortest duration happens to give four here, but it is not reliable in general — a short activity sitting across a busy period can block two others.

questions.q: A student writes a recursive function that returns F(n-1) + F(n-2) and finds it unusably slow for larger n. Which single change turns it into a dynamic programming solution?
options: Store each F(n) when first computed and return the stored value for any later call with the same n
Replace the recursion with a loop that computes F(n-1) + F(n-2) afresh on every pass through the sequence
Compute the first and second halves of the sequence separately and join them at the end
Generate candidate values in order and stop at the first one that satisfies the definition
questions.concept: Dynamic programming is the saving and reuse of sub-problem solutions, not the use of iteration and not decomposition on its own.
questions.why: Dynamic programming breaks a problem into sub-problems and saves their solutions so there is no need to compute a result again; storing each F(n) on first computation is exactly that. A loop that still recomputes each term from scratch changes the control structure without removing the repeated work, and Fibonacci does not split into independent halves.

questions.q: A program must calculate the total cost of an order by adding up the cost of the products and then the VAT. Which arrangement is a pipeline in the sense used in the lesson?
options: One process computes the product subtotal and a second computes the VAT from the original order, and their two outputs are added
One process computes the product subtotal and passes it to a VAT process, whose output goes to a total process
One process stores each product's cost the first time it is looked up so it is not fetched twice
One process tries each candidate total in turn until one matches the sum of the recorded line items
questions.concept: Recognising a pipeline by its serial data dependency — the output of one stage is the input of the next — rather than by the mere presence of several processes.
questions.why: Pipelining divides a task into a series of subtasks where the result of one process feeds into the next until the whole task is complete, which is what the subtotal-then-VAT-then-total chain does. Two processes working from the same original input and combined at the end are independent parts, not a pipeline; caching is dynamic programming and trial of candidates is brute force.

questions.q: A music-centric social network holds three years of five-star song ratings and playlist-sharing records, and wants to find out which of its platform features are used least so it can decide what to retire. Which approach fits?
options: Performance testing, because the question is about how well the individual platform features are working
Hypothesis testing, because two groups of features are being compared
Data mining, because valuable information is extracted from a large data set by finding patterns
Visualisation, because usage figures are best presented as charts
questions.concept: Matching a described situation to the right named approach by what the work actually is, rather than by a surface word in the description.
questions.why: The task is extracting valuable information from a large accumulated data set by discovering patterns and relationships in order to inform a decision, which is the lesson's own definition of data mining and its own example. Performance testing evaluates a program against test scenarios before release, and no prediction is being stated and tested against a null hypothesis here.

questions.q: A student solving a maze generates every complete route from entrance to exit and then checks each one, and the program is far too slow. Which change addresses the actual waste?
options: Divide and conquer: split the maze into quadrants, solve each quadrant, and then join the four partial routes
Greedy: at each junction take the corridor that heads most directly towards the exit and carry on from there
Dynamic programming: store every route already generated so that no route is ever generated a second time
Backtracking: extend a route step by step and, at a dead end, return to the last junction
questions.concept: Diagnosing wasted work: the fault is generating complete candidates that share an already-doomed prefix, which backtracking eliminates by rejecting partial states.
questions.why: Backtracking recognises failure at the dead end and resumes from the previous decision point, discarding in one move every complete route that would have shared that dead end. Storing generated routes does not help because the routes are all distinct, quadrant solutions do not join into valid routes since a corridor may cross a boundary anywhere, and the greedy heading rule can walk confidently into a dead end with no way back.

questions.q: Explain why saving each Fibonacci value the first time it is computed makes such a large difference to the work done, when the arithmetic per term is identical either way.
questions.concept: Overlapping sub-problems: the naive recursion re-derives the same sub-problem many times over, and storage collapses that repetition, not the arithmetic.
questions.why: A full answer must show that the naive recursion for F(n) calls F(n-1) and F(n-2), and that these two calls both go on to require F(n-3), which is therefore computed twice, F(n-4) three times, and so on, so the number of calls grows roughly like the sequence itself. It must then say that dynamic programming saves each result the first time it is produced so that every later request is a lookup, leaving exactly one computation per value of n and one addition each. The point to land is that the saving comes from the sub-problems overlapping — the same F(k) is genuinely needed in many places — and that this is why the arithmetic per term being unchanged is irrelevant to the total cost.

questions.q: Explain why the greedy choice is safe when finding the largest two-digit number from the set 5, 9, 1, 4, 2 and 6, but not when a delivery driver greedily drives to the nearest remaining customer.
questions.concept: A greedy rule is optimal only when the local choice cannot degrade the best completion available afterwards; place value guarantees this, geography does not.
questions.why: A full answer must work the first case: the tens digit is worth ten times the units digit, so any number starting with 9 beats every number starting with anything smaller no matter what follows, and picking 9 then the largest remaining, 6, gives 96. The mechanism is that the first choice is worth more than everything the remaining choices can add up to, so it can never be regretted. It must then contrast the delivery case: taking the nearest stop next can leave the driver at the wrong end of the city with the remaining customers scattered behind, so a small immediate saving buys a large later detour and the total distance is worse. The general statement to reach is that greedy is optimal exactly when the local best cannot rule out a better completion, and that this must be argued for each problem rather than assumed.

questions.q: Explain why the splitting stage of Merge sort does no sorting at all, and where the ordering actually comes from.
questions.concept: In divide and conquer the decomposition only creates trivially solved base cases; the combine step is what produces the answer.
questions.why: A full answer must state that splitting only halves the list repeatedly until each part holds a single element, and that these single-element parts are chosen as the base case precisely because a one-element list is already in order by definition — no comparison has been made at any point during the splitting. It must then locate the work in the merge: two already-ordered lists are combined by repeatedly comparing their front elements and taking the one that belongs first in the target order, so every comparison in the algorithm happens on the way back up. It should draw the divide and conquer moral: the split reduces the problem to something trivially solvable, and the value of the strategy rests on the combine step being cheaper than sorting the original directly.

questions.q: Explain why a food delivery company should not conclude that its new routing program is ready for release simply because it produced correct routes on last month's real orders.
questions.concept: Performance testing requires scenarios chosen against explicit success criteria, including erroneous input and stress conditions, not a single favourable replay.
questions.why: A full answer must say that performance testing means devising a set of test scenarios and success criteria and measuring the program against them before release, so one replay of ordinary historical data is a single scenario with no stated criterion beyond 'it looked right'. It must give the mechanism of the gap: last month's orders contain only the address formats, volumes and road conditions that happened to occur, so the run exercises none of the cases that break routing software. It must name the two kinds of test the lesson specifies — feeding erroneous data, such as malformed or unreachable addresses, to check errors are handled effectively, and simulating real-life extremes such as a peak-hour surge, which is stress testing — and conclude that without measurable success criteria such as maximum route time or fuel cost there is nothing for the result to be judged against.

recapCandidates.topic: The limit of f at a is decided entirely by the values of f at points near a and never by f(a) itself. That is why (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) has the limit 4 at x = 2 even though the function has no value there, and it is the reason cancelling the factor (x - 2) is legitimate rather than a fudge.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students read lim(x to a) f(x) as an instruction to substitute a into f, so they treat the limit as a slow way of computing f(a); the model survives because for polynomials and for rational functions with a non-zero denominator the two really do coincide, and those are most of the examples they meet, so it only breaks at exactly the holes, jumps and 0/0 forms the topic exists to handle.
whyQuestions: Why does the definition insist on 0 < |x - a| rather than just |x - a| < delta?
Why can (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) have a limit of 4 at x = 2 when the function has no value at x = 2?
Why is cancelling the factor (x - 2) legitimate here, when that factor is zero at the very point we are heading towards?
Why does continuity have to be stated as a separate three-part condition instead of following automatically from the limit existing?
Why does this same idea explain what is going on when L'Hopital's Rule is applied to a 0/0 quotient?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It states the punctured-neighbourhood point explicitly: the definition constrains only x with 0 < |x - a| < delta, so f(a) is never consulted and can be changed, or left undefined, without altering the limit.
It uses that to justify cancellation: the reduced function agrees with the original at every x except a, and since limits never look at a, the two functions must have the same limit there.
It separates limit from value with a concrete case of each kind: a hole where the limit exists but f(a) does not, and a jump such as |x|/x at 0 where the one-sided limits disagree so no limit exists at all, and it names continuity as the extra demand that f(a) exists and equals the limit.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Evaluate lim(x to 2) (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2). Step 1, substitute: (4 - 4)/(2 - 2) = 0/0, indeterminate, so substitution is not available and the point x = 2 is not in the domain. Step 2, factor the numerator as a difference of squares: x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2). Step 3, cancel: for every x not equal to 2 the quotient (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) equals x + 2; the cancellation is valid precisely because the limit process only uses x not equal to 2, where (x - 2)/(x - 2) is genuinely 1. Step 4, the reduced function x + 2 is a polynomial, hence continuous, so lim(x to 2) (x + 2) = 4. Therefore the limit is 4. Step 5, interpret: f(2) does not exist, so f is not continuous at 2, but the limit does exist, so the discontinuity is removable; defining f(2) = 4 patches the hole and makes f continuous. Cross-check with L'Hopital: differentiating numerator and denominator separately gives 2x/1, which at x = 2 is 4, the same answer, and for the same reason, namely that both routes strip out the common vanishing factor (x - 2).

recapCandidates.topic: A cell's emf is a fixed property of its chemistry, but the voltage you can measure across its terminals is not: as soon as current flows, a p.d. of Ir is dropped across the cell's own internal resistance and is dissipated inside the cell, so V = epsilon - Ir. Emf is energy supplied per coulomb, and only the part left after the internal loss is delivered to the external circuit.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students treat 'the emf' and 'the battery's voltage' as the same number and solve loops with I = epsilon/R; this survives because in most textbook and lab circuits the external resistance is far larger than r, so V is within a per cent of epsilon and the wrong method still gives nearly the right answer — it only breaks visibly at high current, near short circuit, or in the V-I graph experiment where the whole point is the slope.
whyQuestions: Why is emf measured in volts and not in newtons, if it is called a force?
Why does a voltmeter read 1.5 V across an idle torch cell but only 1.2 V once the bulb is lit?
Why does the loop equation use R + r rather than R alone, when the resistor is the only thing you can see?
Why is the gradient of the V against I graph equal to minus r, and why is the intercept, not the gradient, the emf?
Why does a nearly short-circuited cell get hot while delivering almost no useful power to the external circuit?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Emf is defined as work done per unit charge, epsilon = W/Q, so its unit is the volt (joule per coulomb) and its dimension is M L^2 T^-3 I^-1; it is a property of the source, fixed by its chemistry.
The current in a single loop is the same everywhere, so the emf is shared between the external drop and the internal drop: epsilon = IR + Ir = I(R + r), which rearranges to V = epsilon - Ir; the lost volts Ir are dissipated as heat inside the cell.
The measurement follows from this: V = epsilon - rI is a straight line of gradient -r with V-axis intercept epsilon, so extrapolating to zero current is the only condition under which terminal p.d. and emf coincide.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
A cell of emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected first to R = 2.5 ohm and then to R = 0.10 ohm.
Case 1: I = epsilon/(R + r) = 1.50/(2.5 + 0.50) = 0.50 A. Terminal p.d. V = epsilon - Ir = 1.50 - 0.50 x 0.50 = 1.25 V, and as a check V = IR = 0.50 x 2.5 = 1.25 V. Power to the load = I^2 R = 0.625 W; power wasted inside = I^2 r = 0.125 W.
Case 2: I = 1.50/(0.10 + 0.50) = 2.5 A. V = 1.50 - 2.5 x 0.50 = 0.25 V. Power to the load = I^2 R = 0.625 W, but power wasted inside = I^2 r = 3.13 W — five times more heat in the cell than useful output.
Moral: the same cell, same emf, delivers 1.25 V or 0.25 V depending only on the load, and the naive I = epsilon/R would have predicted 0.60 A and 15 A respectively. Reading the graph back: plotting the two points (0.50 A, 1.25 V) and (2.5 A, 0.25 V) gives gradient (0.25 - 1.25)/(2.5 - 0.50) = -0.50 V/A, so r = 0.50 ohm, and the intercept at I = 0 is 1.50 V, the emf.
